Crucifixion Chronology
kroo-sih-FIK-shun kruh-NOL-oh-jee
noun phrase (the timing of the crucifixion)
From “crucifixion” and “chronology” (Greek chronos, time); the sequence and timing of the events of Christ's death, as recorded in the Gospels.

Biblical Definition

The crucifixion chronology is the sequence and timing of the events of our Lord's death as recorded by the four evangelists—the hours of the day, the darkness, and the relation to the Passover. Mark marks the progress: it was the third hour when they crucified Him; at the sixth hour darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour; and at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?” and gave up the ghost. John, who often reckons by a different scheme, notes that it was the preparation of the passover, about the sixth hour, when Pilate presented Him: “Behold your King!” The supernatural darkness from noon to three, the rending of the temple veil, and the death at the time of the evening sacrifice all belong to the solemn order of that day. The dictionary holds the crucifixion chronology as a matter of the Gospels' historical accuracy and harmony, and as a window into the meaning of the cross. The apparent differences between Mark's “third hour” and John's “sixth hour” are reasonably explained by differing reckonings of time (Jewish from sunrise, Roman or Johannine from midnight) or by the rounding of hours, and do not amount to contradiction; the faithful harmonist finds the accounts complementary, not opposed. The dictionary marks the chronology against the critical assumption that such differences prove the Gospels unreliable, and against the idle over-precision that builds doctrines on a disputed hour. What is sure and central is the substance: at the time of sacrifice, in supernatural darkness, the Lamb of God bore the wrath of God for His people and died, that the veil might be rent and the way into the holiest opened.

Webster 1828 Definition

The sequence and timing of Christ's death in the Gospels—the third, sixth, and ninth hours, the darkness, the Passover (Mark 15:25-34; John 19:14); the apparent hour-differences harmonized by differing reckonings, against the claim that they prove the Gospels unreliable.

CRUCIFIXION CHRONOLOGY, noun phrase. The sequence and timing of the events of Christ's death in the Gospels.

“It was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mark 15:25).

Darkness covered the land from the sixth to the ninth hour (Mark 15:33).

At the ninth hour He cried, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34).

John notes the preparation of the passover, about the sixth hour (John 19:14).

Key Scripture

Mr 15:25 — "And it was the third hour, and they crucified him."

Mr 15:33 — "And when the sixth hour was come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour."

Mr 15:34 — "And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"

Joh 19:14 — "And it was the preparation of the passover, and about the sixth hour: and he saith unto the Jews, Behold your King!"

Modern Corruption

The critical school treats the apparent hour-differences as proof that the Gospels contradict and are unreliable, while an idle over-precision builds doctrines on a disputed hour.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the harmony and reliability of the Gospels. The critical school seizes on the apparent difference between Mark's “third hour” of the crucifixion and John's “sixth hour” at the judgment as proof that the evangelists contradict and that Scripture errs. The dictionary answers that the difference is reasonably resolved: the evangelists may reckon hours by differing conventions (the Jewish day from sunrise, the Johannine perhaps from midnight), and ancient reckoning rounded to the nearest third of the day. The accounts are complementary witnesses, not contradictions; the faithful reader harmonizes rather than impugns.

The opposite error is an idle over-precision that builds large conclusions on a disputed hour or insists on a rigid timetable the texts do not supply. The dictionary counsels sobriety here too: the Gospels were not written to satisfy the stopwatch but to bear true witness, and they agree in all that matters. What is sure and central is the substance of the day—the supernatural darkness from noon to three, the cry of dereliction, the death at the hour of the evening sacrifice, the rending of the veil. On these the four agree, and on these the dictionary rests: the Lamb of God died in darkness, bearing the wrath of God, and opened the way into the holiest.

Hebrew Roots

From chronos (time) applied to the crucifixion; the Gospels mark the “hours” (Greek hora) of the day, reckoned by differing conventions.

expand to see more

Hora, Greek, “hour,” the divisions of the daylight reckoned in the Gospels.

The Jewish day was counted from sunrise; the “third hour” thus near nine in the morning.

John may reckon from midnight, placing the “sixth hour” near dawn.

The darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour (noon to three) was supernatural.

The death near the ninth hour coincided with the time of the evening sacrifice.

Usage

"The teacher harmonized Mark's and John's hours by differing conventions of reckoning time."

"He warned against impugning the Gospels over a rounded hour, and against building doctrines on it."

"She fixed her eyes on the substance: the Lamb dying in darkness at the hour of sacrifice."
